speaker: Michael Truell
title: Michael Truell: How Cursor Builds at the Speed of AI
question: Why does keeping an open-ended multi-day work trial past 200 employees outperform standard technical interview loops?
guest: Normally when you are a small company, you have your first engineers contract with you instead of doing a LeetCode-style interview loop, because you are getting to the ground truth of whether you work well together. Usually companies stop doing that after a couple of hires, but we still have everyone hired on engineering and design spend two days in the office working on a freeform project. It is a frozen older version of the codebase with DevEx set up—just go do it. That serves three functions. First, it tests orthogonal things to standard coding interviews: can they go end-to-end in the codebase, are they agentic, and what do they build if left in a vacuum without a team, which reveals product sense. Second, it functions as a culture interview over four to six meals together. Third, it gives the candidate huge information about what day one actually feels like, leading to much higher fit on their end if they say yes.

points.core: Freeform codebase projects measure end-to-end agency that standard coding interviews miss.
points.note: Accept: noting that working on a real/frozen codebase with minimal structure tests orthogonal traits like end-to-end navigation, autonomy, or agency missed by algorithmic/whiteboard loops. Do not credit: generic statements that "work samples are more realistic" without specifying end-to-end execution or agency.

points.core: Unstructured project work reveals whether engineers possess independent product judgment.
points.note: Accept: observing what a candidate chooses to build when left without hand-holding exposes product sense or taste for tightly coupled product-engineering roles. Do not credit: conflating product judgment with pure code correctness or syntax speed.

points.core: Extended shared meals provide realistic culture signal beyond rehearsed behavioral interviews.
points.note: Accept: spending multiple informal meals/days together gives authentic mutual signal on day-to-day interpersonal compatibility. Do not credit: generic mentions of "cultural fit" without linking it to extended unscripted interaction.

points.core: Realistic day-one immersion helps candidates self-select for stronger mutual fit.
points.note: Accept: giving candidates accurate firsthand exposure to the real work environment lets them evaluate the company honestly, improving post-offer acceptance quality and retention. Do not credit: framing the trial solely as a one-sided employer filter.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
The premise isn't established: there is no rigorous evidence that open-ended multi-day work trials outperform standard interview loops, at 200 employees or any other size. I'm answering from memory rather than a fresh search.

What supports the idea is that work-sample tests are among the better predictors of job performance in the selection research (Schmidt & Hunter 1998; Sackett et al. 2022). A trial also shows things interviews measure poorly, such as collaboration, communication, handling ambiguity and working in a real codebase. Companies such as Automattic and PostHog use paid trials well beyond 200 people and say they work well, but that is self-reported and not a controlled comparison.

The case against grows with scale. Sackett's re-analysis put structured interviews at roughly the same or better validity than work samples. Open-ended trials are hard to standardise, so evaluations become noisier and more bias-prone as more teams run them. They also cost considerable employee time, and they screen out candidates who can't take days off from a current job or caregiving, which narrows and skews the pool.

Trials can work if they are paid, structured and consistently scored, but "outperforms" is a claim, not a finding.

points.why: The response mentions handling ambiguity and working in a real codebase without explaining how the trial reveals autonomous, end-to-end execution.
The response never links what candidates choose to build to their independent product judgment.
The response mentions collaboration and communication without explaining how extended informal interaction reveals day-to-day cultural compatibility.
The response never explains how firsthand exposure helps candidates decide whether the company is a good fit for them.

models.answer:
Standard technical interview loops measure rehearsed performance on narrow, artificial prompts, which are easily gamed and increasingly blurred by AI tools. In contrast, an open-ended, multi-day work trial embeds candidates into the real codebase and team workflow, directly testing what interviews only proxy: high agency, product taste, iteration speed, and day-to-day collaboration. Keeping the work open-ended is crucial because tightly scoped tasks only test execution, whereas ambiguity reveals how an engineer frames problems, navigates unfamiliar systems, responds to feedback, and exercises judgment as requirements evolve.

Most companies drop trials before reaching 200 employees to streamline hiring volume with standardized rubrics, inadvertently diluting talent density right when organizational complexity spikes. Maintaining the trial past that inflection point acts as a forcing function that protects engineering standards, reinforces cultural buy-in from peers who passed the same bar, and prevents costly mis-hires. Equally important, side-by-side real work provides two-way signal, helping close elite candidates who distrust contrived whiteboard exercises and want firsthand proof of a team’s velocity, autonomy, and caliber.

noweb.answer:
Past 200 employees, day-to-day work shifts from greenfield building to navigating sprawling codebases, cross-team dependencies, and organizational ambiguity. Standard technical interview loops are usually adopted at this stage because they scale predictably, yet they test isolated puzzles and rehearsed system-design scripts rather than the judgment required in a growing company. Keeping an open-ended, multi-day work trial lets an organization directly observe real-world execution: how candidates scope underspecified problems, comprehend unfamiliar systems, communicate asynchronously, incorporate feedback, and balance speed against quality.

At this headcount, hiring mistakes also become harder to spot and costlier to unwind, as underperformers can blend into larger teams while quietly eroding velocity and standards. Work trials sharply reduce false positives—candidates who excel at interview prep but stall without rigid specifications—while surfacing pragmatic builders whom timed coding tests filter out. Trials also create two-way transparency, giving strong candidates an honest look at actual workflows and culture before committing. Provided candidates are compensated fairly and evaluated against consistent rubrics, the superior predictive signal of a work trial easily outweighs its operational overhead.

models.answer:
The question assumes something that hasn't been shown. No rigorous evidence says multi-day work trials beat structured interview loops, at 200 employees or any other size. The best-known companies that run them, such as Automattic, PostHog and Linear, describe their own success, but none has published controlled comparisons. Research on selection methods, starting with Schmidt and Hunter's meta-analyses, does find that work samples and structured interviews predict job performance relatively well. Work trials are essentially long work samples, so the idea is plausible but unproven.

Supporters argue that trials show real behavior: how someone handles ambiguity, communicates asynchronously, asks questions and finishes realistic tasks. Puzzle-style interviews mostly reward rehearsed performance. Trials also let candidates judge the company, which may reduce early attrition.

The costs grow with headcount. Trials take a lot of team time. They screen out people who can't take several days off, often those with current jobs or caregiving duties. They're hard to standardize, which leaves room for bias. If you keep trials as you grow, they work best paid, tightly scoped, scored with consistent rubrics and checked against later performance data, rather than simply assumed to be better.

The response explicitly says the trial gives candidates a basis for judging the company and links that judgment to potentially lower early attrition.

models.answer:
Standard technical interview loops rely on short, contrived exercises that measure test-taking and recall rather than how someone actually builds software. An open-ended multi-day work trial replaces those noisy proxies with direct evidence of real job performance: how a candidate scopes ambiguity, navigates an unfamiliar codebase, makes product and engineering trade-offs, responds to feedback, and ships working solutions under realistic constraints.

Keeping this practice past 200 employees is especially valuable because growing organizations tend to trade hiring signal for standardized throughput, which quietly dilutes the engineering bar and culture. Embedding finalists with the team for several days exposes collaboration style, ownership, taste, and velocity in ways forty-five-minute interviews cannot, dramatically reducing costly mis-hires. It also works as a two-way filter: candidates experience the company's real pace, tooling, and teammates before accepting, which strengthens mutual conviction, accelerates onboarding, and improves retention. Although harder to coordinate at scale, the compounding value of consistently high-signal hires far outweighs the logistical friction.

noweb.answer:
Standard technical interview loops measure a narrow, rehearsed proxy for the job: solving contrived problems under artificial time pressure. Once a company passes 200 employees, those standardized loops often degrade into rubric-checking that rewards polished interviewees while missing what actually drives impact at scale. An open-ended, multi-day work trial outperforms them because it directly samples the real work. Rather than testing whether someone can recall an algorithm on a whiteboard, it reveals how they navigate ambiguity, scope an underspecified problem, orient themselves in an unfamiliar codebase, and make pragmatic engineering tradeoffs.

At that size, coordination and judgment matter as much as raw coding ability. Working together over several days exposes how a candidate communicates in writing, incorporates feedback, unblocks themselves, and collaborates with future teammates—signals that are nearly impossible to fake or observe in 45-minute interviews. It also gives candidates an honest preview of the culture and tooling, preventing expensive mis-hires and early attrition that compound quickly as an organization scales.

models.answer:
At Linear, a paid two-to-five-day work trial gives the team a better view of how a candidate would do the job. An open-ended project leaves real decisions to the candidate. The team can see which questions they ask, what they prioritize, how they explain tradeoffs, and how they revise their work after feedback. A standard technical interview can test coding and system design, but short, separate rounds offer fewer chances to see those skills come together in day-to-day work. The candidate also gets to see how the team actually operates. [Linear’s account of its work trials](https://linear.app/now/why-and-how-we-do-work-trials-at-linear)

The case for keeping the trial past 200 employees is that those observations still matter as hiring scales. Using the trial as a paid final stage keeps the time commitment focused on finalists. Linear’s experience illustrates why the format can work at scale, though it does not establish that trials produce better hires at every company. [Linear’s hiring process](https://linear.app/now/how-we-hire-at-linear)

noweb.answer:
An open-ended, multi-day work trial can outperform a standard technical interview loop because it samples the work the company is actually hiring someone to do. A candidate has time to clarify an ambiguous problem, decide what matters, make trade-offs, and revise their approach after feedback. The team can assess the result and the judgment behind it. A timed interview gives candidates fewer chances to show how they work through those decisions, and performance can depend heavily on familiarity with the format.

Past 200 employees, the trial also gives hiring teams concrete evidence they can compare using a shared rubric as more people get involved in hiring. Candidates get a firsthand look at how the team works, too. The extra time pays off when the task reflects the role, reviewers score it consistently, and the trial is paid and flexible enough for candidates to participate.

It can outperform a standard technical interview loop when success in the role depends on judgment and collaboration as much as coding speed. Over several days, a candidate can clarify an ambiguous problem, choose what to build, explain a tradeoff, and revise their work after feedback. Interviewers can see how those decisions play out, and the candidate gets a realistic sense of working with the team.

Crossing 200 employees doesn’t make that evidence less valuable. What changes is the cost of collecting it consistently. A paid, time-bounded trial with shared scoring criteria can preserve the benefit as hiring grows. An unpaid or loosely scored trial can instead favor candidates with spare time or those whose style resembles the team’s. Whether it actually outperforms interviews depends on how well it predicts later job performance and which qualified candidates drop out.
